title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
text:
ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni requires independent customer companies with branches, memberships, media and devices. The derived repository has PostgreSQL infrastructure and composable API modules but no product tables or tenant enforcement. Tenant isolation must exist in the first product slice, within Orion's modular backend boundaries.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt one customer company as the tenant ownership boundary in a shared PostgreSQL database and schema. Model explicit tenant-scoped ownership and references, server-derived membership/branch authorization, and database constraints that prevent cross-tenant associations. Keep capabilities in the existing modular backend, with explicit application interfaces and owned tables; no microservice split is proposed.
Row-level security is an additional option to evaluate, not assumed protection. Review its connection-pooling, runtime-role and migration implications before selecting it. Platform administration remains a separate scoped capability, not an implicit bypass for tenant data access.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
A shared deployment fits the initial cost and operational constraints. Explicit ownership allows branch scoping and future company scale without treating a branch as another tenant. It also places substantial responsibility on query/reference design, constraints and adversarial authorization tests; the accepted architecture has not yet been proven by a schema or implementation.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Database or schema per company:** provides a different isolation boundary, but adds migration, connection, backup and recovery coordination for every tenant. Revisit if contractual isolation or measured scale justifies it.
**Application filters without relational tenant constraints:** simpler initially, but insufficient to protect mixed-tenant references or accidental omitted scope checks. Not a sufficient candidate for the product requirement.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Preserves one operational backend while giving each module clear ownership and tenant semantics.
Enables negative integration tests against real PostgreSQL from the first vertical slice.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Every data access, reference, cache, media path and asynchronous operation must preserve scope.
Isolation in a shared database requires continuing review; application administrator access and recovery operations remain sensitive.

title: ADR-0018: Adopt Tenant-Owned Data in the Modular Backend
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No tables or migrations are introduced by this decision. Before dependent implementation/release, complete the ownership/constraint design and row-level-security evaluation and verify the selected role matrix with cross-tenant tests under PJ-03/PJ-07. Later changing tenant partitioning may require a deliberate data migration.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
text:
ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni displays must continue through temporary backend/network outages. Videos must normally play locally. Partial downloads, concurrent publications and power loss must not replace usable programming with an incomplete set. Backend and installed players will evolve independently.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt immutable publication snapshots with versioned manifests that bind programming rules to verified asset versions. The player durably stages missing assets and switches its active generation only after the complete supported snapshot is ready, retaining a valid recovery generation. Separate desired, staged and reported-active versions and reconcile duplicate or lost acknowledgements.
Define protocol compatibility, integrity metadata, capacity/retention, scheduling expiry and offline authorization policy before implementation. No transport, storage library, cryptographic mechanism or manifest serialization format is selected by this record.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
The owner's requirement is consistent offline playback, not normal continuous server streaming. A generation boundary makes interruption and recovery behavior testable and avoids exposing partially updated programming. Architectural acceptance is not evidence of crash-safe storage or hardware compatibility.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Continuous server streaming:** makes ordinary playback depend on connectivity and repeated transfer; does not satisfy the central offline requirement.
**Overwrite active files/programming as downloads arrive:** reduces temporary storage but can mix incompatible versions and leave no valid program after interruption. It does not satisfy the required activation boundary.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Enables local replay through outages and explicit recovery/failure acceptance tests.
Separates publication intent from device observations without assuming exactly-once delivery.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Staging plus recovery versions consume additional storage and need safe garbage collection.
Cached content cannot be immediately recalled from unreachable devices; expiry/revocation rules need explicit review.

title: ADR-0019: Adopt Immutable Publications and Atomic Player Activation
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Atomicity across PostgreSQL and media storage needs durable intent/reconciliation. The player needs proven local activation durability and a supported backend/player overlap. Player/release qualification under PJ-11/PJ-12/PJ-14 requires representative network/power-cut and stale/reordered message cases, not only unit tests.

heading: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
text:
ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Context
text:
Context
The intended first player is Android TV, with continuous image/video playback, local persistence, temporary-code pairing and offline recovery. Orion supplies TypeScript API/web foundations but deliberately does not select a mobile/native stack. No Android application or hardware validation exists in Teluni.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt an independently built/distributed native Android TV player using Kotlin and Android Media3/ExoPlayer, with durable local media/configuration/synchronization state. Consume versioned backend HTTP contracts; do not import backend or web implementation. Keep player credentials in reviewed platform-protected storage.
Minimum platform version, supported devices/codecs/orientations, persistence library, packaging, startup/unattended behavior and controlled update/rollback mechanisms remain pending validation. Architecture acceptance does not imply every Android TV or Smart TV is supported.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
This is the owner's preferred initial direction and matches the requested native device lifecycle and local-playback responsibilities. There are no completed benchmarks or device tests establishing that it meets the reliability envelope. A separate runtime is justified by installation and hardware lifecycle, while backend distribution is not.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Web player first:** remains a possible future platform, but browser lifecycle, storage and unattended playback would need separate validation. It is not the requested MVP target.
**Other Smart TV or dedicated-computer players:** could expand coverage later; validating multiple platforms now would widen MVP support and test obligations without pilot evidence.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Gives the first player a clear device-specific owner and keeps interoperable contracts with Orion.
Allows targeted validation of local storage, playback and restart behavior on pilot hardware.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Adds Android build/signing/distribution, hardware testing and old-client compatibility responsibilities.
Media capability and unattended behavior must be verified per supported device; TypeScript tooling cannot establish them.

title: ADR-0020: Adopt a Native Android TV Player
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Supported-device/release qualification under PH-08/PJ-12/PJ-14 requires the pilot hardware matrix, chosen installation/update policy and playback/reboot/power-loss evidence. No application directory, Gradle project, dependency or signing credential is created in this documentation stage.

heading: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
text:
ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Context
text:
Context
The owner currently has no cloud-service budget and intends to evaluate a personal residential server for development and first pilots. Network exposure, CGNAT, domain, hardware capacity, backup destination and acceptable downtime have not been verified. Orion does not select a production deployment platform.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt an initial Debian host with Docker Compose, HTTPS reverse-proxy ingress, private PostgreSQL and media on durable mounted storage outside disposable containers. Keep environment-specific endpoints/configuration out of domain identity. Media storage remains a cohesive capability with replaceable filesystem I/O, allowing a later S3-compatible implementation when justified.
Real-customer exposure is conditional on network/security review, owner-approved availability and recovery targets, off-host backup/restore proof and tested player behavior during outages. No tunnel, DNS, proxy, object-storage or cloud provider is selected or presumed to satisfy these gates.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
One host and local media fit the stated budget and avoid premature distributed operations. Stable logical asset identity, explicit configuration and tested recovery make a host/storage move tractable. They do not remove single-host failure or bandwidth constraints, nor make a future migration automatic.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Immediate paid VPS/cloud:** potentially changes power/network risk, but needs an actual affordable operating budget. Revisit with revenue or a demonstrated operational requirement.
**Distributed services or orchestration first:** adds deployment and failure-management costs without measured need at the initial pilot scope.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Keeps the first operating model understandable and limits mandatory paid infrastructure.
Establishes persistent state and endpoint portability as design obligations before deployment.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Residential availability, uplink and physical security remain material risks; no production SLA follows from Compose.
Database-plus-media consistency, off-host recovery, secure exposure and maintenance remain owner/operator responsibilities.

title: ADR-0021: Adopt a Single-Host Pilot with Portable Persistent Storage
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Real-customer deployment readiness under PH-10/PJ-13 requires the host/network inventory, endpoint migration strategy and timed recovery rehearsal. Implementation must later supply tested deployment/recovery runbooks and release procedures. No container manifest or production change is introduced here.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
text:
ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-17

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni is derived from Orion, whose source already carries Apache-2.0 under ADR-0016. That foundation decision explicitly leaves independently developed product licensing to the product owner. Teluni's owner explicitly approved Apache License 2.0 for Teluni on 2026-10-17; this record documents that owner-authorized decision. The repository already contains the standard root license text, but its README and human actions previously said product licensing was undecided.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
License Teluni repository source and documentation, including independently developed product material, under the unmodified Apache License, Version 2.0. Retain the root `LICENSE` as the canonical terms and use SPDX identifier `Apache-2.0` in the root, API, web and SDK package metadata. Update README and project documentation to make the scope explicit.
Preserve Orion provenance and its applicable rights/notices. Do not relabel third-party dependencies or separately licensed material. Do not invent a named copyright holder or NOTICE without confirmed attribution. This decision concerns repository licensing; SaaS pricing, support and customer service terms remain separate product decisions.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
The owner explicitly selected Apache-2.0 rather than delegating the legal choice to an agent. Applying the existing standard text consistently to Teluni resolves the previous distinction between inherited foundation licensing and undecided product licensing, without changing architecture or runtime behavior.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Keep product licensing undecided
text:
Keep product licensing undecided
This was the documented state. It no longer reflects the owner's explicit instruction and leaves the intended licensing scope unclear.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Teluni's source/documentation license is explicit and consistent with the standard license file and package metadata.
The product decision remains separate from the historical Orion ADR and commercial pricing decisions.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Distribution must preserve applicable license/attribution obligations; the choice does not determine third-party rights or authorize reuse of PDT Display material.
Named attribution still needs confirmed ownership evidence if such notices are added.

title: ADR-0022: License Teluni under Apache-2.0
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No database migration, dependency upgrade, application feature or deployment change is required. Existing tags/history and the canonical license text remain unchanged. PH-06 records the owner's selection; PH-14 tracks conditional named-attribution work.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
text:
ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Context
text:
Context
The owner requires freeform simultaneous content, regional schedules with optional page coordination, multiple videos/audio and configurable data catalogs beyond products, such as weekly agendas. Saving designated prices must automatically publish affected content, while other drafts remain private. Players must render locally through bounded outages and recover complete valid generations.
These approved product policies affect schema evolution, references, module ownership and backend/web/player contracts. They do not choose a physical schema, editor/renderer, serialization or queue provider. ADR-0019 establishes immutable publication generations; the expanded presentation/data boundary needs explicit design review before implementation.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt versioned declarative composition definitions and typed catalog definitions/records with stable field/binding identities. Customization is validated data rather than executable user code or direct database access. Catalog presets may express products/prices or agendas without making a product schema mandatory for every collection.
Compose immutable publication snapshots from explicitly identified layout/schema/record/media revisions and the rules needed for offline evaluation. Published snapshots remain interpretable after draft schema evolution. A price save records durable intent and generates affected snapshots from published dependencies, excluding unrelated drafts; expose incomplete/retry states and prevent stale work from overwriting newer desired generations.
Keep catalogs, layout authoring, programming and publication behind explicit module capabilities in the modular backend. No arbitrary cross-module table writes, circular imports or new generic shared framework are implied. Carry interoperable contracts to the native player rather than importing TypeScript application internals.
Before dependent implementation, review concrete schemas, module collaboration, import security, destructive field evolution, snapshot granularity, trusted time, rendering/media profiles and the failure/compatibility fixtures. Serialization, storage layout, libraries and processing/transport mechanisms remain intentionally unselected.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
User-defined fields and freeform geometry need stable meaning across independent editor/player releases. A versioned declarative boundary makes validation, copying, private references and offline rendering reviewable. Immutable data snapshots preserve the existing consistency/activation direction while allowing automatic price updates without live mutation of an issued program.
This is reasoned architecture, not a measured renderer/storage evaluation. PH-09 policy selection alone did not accept this ADR; explicit architectural approval is recorded above. Neither establishes product availability.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Product-only fixed fields and opaque final artwork:** cannot satisfy configurable non-product catalogs, field-bound editing and independent regional presentation without rebuilding the model.
**Read mutable live records while rendering an old publication:** makes ordinary playback depend on the server or mixes data/layout/schema revisions; obscures rollback and offline commercial validity.
**Unversioned arbitrary catalog/layout objects:** initially flexible but leaves incompatible field changes, unsafe references and preview/player interpretation undefined. Extensibility still needs typed validation and compatibility rules.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Supports sector-neutral catalogs, reusable textual layouts and controlled offline interpretation.
Keeps ordinary drafts separate from explicit automatic price publication and preserves attributable generation history.
Makes schema/reference/security and regional scheduling cases part of contract verification.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Requires schema evolution/reference handling and qualified multi-area/video rendering across independent runtimes.
Publication fan-out, processing and retained generations add storage/work and recovery obligations.
Does not remove real device limits, trusted-time uncertainty or the inability to erase an unreachable player instantly.

title: ADR-0023: Adopt Versioned Catalog and Composition Publications
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No product schema or deployment currently exists, so this decision adds no migration or running component. Future implementations must keep retained snapshots readable, reconcile interrupted price/publication work and qualify protocol overlap, offline/power recovery and supported device profiles. Apply accepted ADR-0019 alongside this record; neither supersedes an earlier foundation decision.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
text:
ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Context
text:
Context
The owner answered PH-11's identity questionnaire, selecting self-hosted Keycloak as candidate, email/password with optional passkeys, Google as the only external login, and server-managed browser sessions. Public company activation, strong administrative assurance, safe recovery and bounded revocation must work within an initially unfunded residential deployment. A concrete provider/version has not been provisioned or qualified.
Accepted ADR-0012 governs the existing API's signed JWT access-token boundary. Its header/claims are not ordinary provider defaults, and its current principal result does not expose session or authentication-assurance evidence. The web shell's in-memory bearer support is not a login/refresh implementation. This decision must distinguish product-policy approval from technical acceptance and implementation.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt Keycloak as the human identity provider, self-hosted subject to PH-10 feasibility, with a server-managed browser session integrated into the modular backend where appropriate. Use established OIDC Authorization Code with PKCE and maintained session/security components; keep provider credentials server-side and an opaque protected session cookie in the browser. Do not introduce a new microservice by default or an API-owned password/cryptographic implementation.
Preserve ADR-0012's API boundary and stable application principal. A reviewed session boundary must obtain legitimate issuer access tokens and establish trusted session/assurance context; a cookie or caller-supplied MFA/session assertion cannot bypass the existing verifier. Define protected cookies, explicit CSRF protection, OIDC state/nonce/redirect validation, session fixation defenses, refresh rotation/replay/concurrency and local/global logout reconciliation before implementation. No session library, route, schema or deployment image is selected by this decision. The pinned Keycloak source assessment in the provider evaluation is review evidence, not an installed production version.
Apply the owner's canonical identity policies, including strong/recent authentication, distinct platform accounts, recovery, inactivity/absolute expiry, session-count and 30-second revocation requirements. Current account/session/membership state must supplement JWT verification. Keep Google brokering/account linking and provider/email credentials at trusted boundaries. A human actor mapper must not accidentally make machine flows authenticate as humans.
The [pinned-source compatibility assessment](../project/identity-provider-evaluation.md#pinned-source-assessment) supports this architectural choice. Before integration readiness, implement and verify immutable principal mapping, every required token claim and trusted session/assurance linkage against the selected deployment version using the remaining qualification cases. Where evidence is insufficient, retain an explicit qualification task; do not modify accepted checks to make a default provider token pass. Review deployment/recovery resources separately under PH-10/PH-15. This decision neither supersedes ADR-0012 nor authorizes provisioning.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
The provider matches the owner's control/budget direction and has relevant documented identity primitives. Server-managed sessions reduce browser exposure of provider tokens and permit accountable session lifecycle controls, at the cost of persistent state and CSRF/refresh coordination. A five-minute token alone cannot enforce the selected 30-second revocation bound. Local JWT verification can remain useful without pretending it provides a complete session or authorization system.
The documentation review establishes plausible compatibility, including Keycloak's configurable `at+jwt` header, not passed interoperability, recovery or capacity tests. Public signup still needs commercial/privacy and abuse readiness; choosing it does not authorize a free plan or immediate public exposure.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Managed OIDC provider:** may reduce some operating responsibilities, but costs/limits/claim compatibility require evaluation beyond the current no-procurement direction. No vendor benchmark or unconditional free-tier assumption is made.
**Browser-token SPA with Authorization Code and PKCE:** preserves a simpler server session topology but leaves browser token exposure and refresh/lifecycle tradeoffs; the owner selected server-managed sessions instead. This does not reject the client-first React/Vite application or require server rendering.
**Another established self-hosted provider:** fallback if qualification rejects Keycloak; no unperformed comparative assessment is claimed.
**Custom issuer/password storage or relaxed JWT checks:** violates governing controls and is not an acceptable workaround.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Keeps human credentials with an established provider and browser tokens out of JavaScript-accessible persistence.
Preserves provider-independent identity and explicit failure/revocation/assurance boundaries.
Defines compatibility and operational evidence before a production integration is claimed.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Self-hosting adds patching, resources, recovery and mail-delivery responsibilities despite no procurement budget.
Server sessions introduce persistence, CSRF, concurrency and logout synchronization work.
Current foundation principal/configuration contracts do not yet carry all needed session/assurance semantics.

title: ADR-0024: Adopt Keycloak and Server-Managed Human Sessions
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No runtime, dependency, API contract, migration or deployment changes accompany this decision. Future delivery must pin a maintained provider version/image, define protected credentials/configuration, qualify claim/assurance/session behavior and reconcile revocations on restore. Provider migration preserves application IDs but may require password resets or factor reenrollment. PH-15–PH-17 track external identity, Google and mail prerequisites; PH-11 decision acceptance is complete; PJ-24 retains every unperformed interoperability/session/assurance test.

heading: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles

ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved all pending Teluni ADRs on 2026-10-18. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction, not implementation or production readiness. The design reviews, security controls and qualification evidence below remain mandatory delivery gates in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md).

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Context
text:
Context
PH-11 approved multiple company memberships, branch-specific grants, customizable profiles and explicit resource sharing. A designated responsible administrator approves additional administrators. The backend must enforce the selected role matrix, strong authentication, 30-second revocation and publication impact, including automatically published prices. Company administration and platform operation must not imply unrestricted customer-content support.
The foundation verifies human identity but has no product membership/permission implementation. ADR-0018 establishes the accepted tenant-owned modular-data direction; its concrete constraints/enforcement remain design and implementation work. Provider-native groups or immutable token roles alone cannot express current resource scope, temporary grants and all-target price effects safely.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Adopt application-owned memberships, explicit scoped capability grants and company-customized profiles, with readable standard role presets. Scope grants to a company and explicit branches/resources; combine valid grants additively within their scopes. Account/membership suspension and grant expiration deny access regardless of profile labels. No implicit access to future branches, arbitrary negative-rule language, cyclic inheritance or universal administrator shortcut is selected.
Keep authorization meaning with the owning application/module capabilities; identity/provider adapters establish trusted principals and assurance but do not own company permissions. The organizations capability owns membership/profile meaning. Modules use explicit public capabilities for authorization facts rather than arbitrary cross-module table reads or a generic global switch over domain rules. Exact schema, persistence constraints, caching/invalidation and any row-level-security design require review with ADR-0018 before implementation. No external permission engine or shared framework is selected.
Enforce resource ownership, operation, current state, assurance and scope on every protected entry point, including reads/collections, media, imports, bulk work and delayed effects. Revalidate sensitive effects and ensure the selected freshness bound. Grantors cannot delegate authority they lack, responsible-administrator approval cannot be bypassed, and local membership administration cannot reset global identities.
Authorize every published dependency/target affected by a price save before accepting the mutation; deny the entire out-of-scope mutation without partial publication or automatic approval fallback. Optional company approval policies distinguish a proposal from an effective saved price and prohibit self-approval where required. Pending protected work rechecks authority; an already-issued valid publication continues its delivery lifecycle unless explicitly revoked by the appropriate control.
Routine support uses the real support identity and a visible, expiring customer-authorized scope, read-only by default and separate write grants. No impersonation is selected. Emergency access requires a separately reviewed, exceptional controlled procedure; there is no standing unrestricted content-browsing right.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
Application ownership keeps mutable company permissions and resources independent of provider migration and stale identity claims. Explicit capabilities/scopes accommodate both small-business presets and teams working across branches without making every operator an administrator. Attributable publication/support checks preserve the approved product behavior and tenant boundaries.
The owner approved policy and required allow/deny cases, not a database model or proven permission evaluator. Custom profiles, optional approvals and bounded asynchronous revocation add real implementation work and must not be claimed merely from a matrix.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Alternatives Considered
text:
Alternatives Considered
**Fixed roles only:** simpler, but cannot satisfy the selected customizable capability/scoping policy without revisiting the product requirements.
**Provider roles/groups as complete authorization:** insufficient for current memberships, mutable resource relationships, publication fan-out and tenant-safe support; would couple application permission meaning to identity infrastructure.
**General-purpose policy engine:** no measured need or evaluation justifies another dependency or distributed component at this stage. Review if actual policy complexity warrants it later.
**Platform superuser and silent price partial success:** obscure authority and violate selected customer-content boundaries and complete price-impact validation.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
Makes granted authority, tenant/resource scope, responsibility and delegated support explainable and testable.
Keeps identity migration independent from company permission ownership.
Preserves safe all-target publication and attributable pending-work behavior.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Custom profiles, shared resources and optional approvals increase UX, schema and test complexity.
Freshness, grant races and background work require explicit consistency/invalidation design.
A safe role matrix alone cannot prevent unsafe queries, caches or credential mapping.

title: ADR-0025: Adopt Application-Owned Scoped Access Profiles
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
No permission identifiers, schema, migration or running engine is created here. Implementation/release qualification under PJ-03/PJ-07/PJ-24 requires reviewed capability ownership, consistency/enforcement design and passing IA-01–IA-16 cases, including two-company negative fixtures and trustworthy session/assurance context. Later renaming persisted grants or broadening presets is a compatibility/security change. Audit/privacy retention and host recovery remain separate gates.

heading: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
text:
ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-18
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the D-13 design on 2026-10-18 under PH-21. Acceptance establishes the architectural direction for local and CI implementation, not production readiness. Real sending still requires PH-17's sender, domain authentication and provider terms and PH-13's notices and retention, and the qualification evidence in the [implementation plan](../project/implementation-plan.md) remains mandatory.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Context
text:
Context
Company invitations are the first Teluni workflow that must send email from the application: the selected identity policy requires recipient-bound, single-use invitations valid for seven days, and later notices will need the same capability. Keycloak sends its own verification and recovery messages but cannot send application messages, and memberships and grants are application-owned (ADR-0025).
The [delivery policy](../architecture/delivery-and-side-effects.md) requires a durable required side effect to record its intent with the state change, since sending after commit can lose the effect in a crash and sending before commit can announce a change that never happened. The API currently has no background processing, message broker or outbound-email path. Deployment is a single residential host with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL (ADR-0021), with no recurring procurement budget for identity or email services yet (P03). The real provider, sender domain and DNS authentication are not selected (PH-17), and legal retention is not set (PH-13).
This record decides the delivery mechanism. The invitation rules, credential handling, limits and retention proposals are specified in the [invitation and email delivery design](../project/invitation-delivery-design.md) (D-13).

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will deliver transactional email through an application-owned outbox in PostgreSQL and an authenticated SMTP relay:
A dedicated API capability owns an outbound-message table, a dispatcher and an SMTP adapter. Producers enqueue a message in the same database transaction as the business change it reports, through that capability's public port, and can cancel a message they enqueued. The producing capability owns the meaning of a message; the mail capability owns only delivery.
The dispatcher runs inside the API process. It claims due messages with row locks and `SKIP LOCKED` under expiring leases, submits them through SMTP, and records sent, failed or cancelled outcomes with bounded retries, so several instances never send one claim twice in normal operation.
Delivery is at least once. A crash between the relay's acceptance and the local record can send a message again; consumers of the email (people following a link) must tolerate repeats, and exactly-once delivery is not claimed.
The SMTP client is the established `nodemailer` library. The relay is provider-neutral and configured, with TLS required in production; a provider's proprietary HTTP API or webhooks are not used in this version.
Message bodies are rendered from fixed templates when sent. Secret parameters are stored encrypted under a dedicated key ring only until the message is final. Recipient addresses and credentials never reach logs or telemetry.
No message broker, separate worker service or job-queue library is introduced. Bounce processing, delivery receipts and a separate worker deployment remain possible later without changing producers.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
PostgreSQL is already the system of record and provides transactional enqueueing and concurrent claiming, so the producer's change and its email commit or fail together without a second stateful system on the single host. In-process dispatch adds no deployment unit; when the API is down, messages wait rather than disappear, which fits low pilot volume and residential availability. Leases and `SKIP LOCKED` keep the design correct if more instances run later.
SMTP submission is the most widely supported provider interface, which keeps PH-17 free to choose any service, including one already available to the owner, and keeps a provider change to configuration. `nodemailer` is the long-established Node.js SMTP client and avoids writing protocol code; it is a routine dependency added under the normal review and supply-chain rules.
At-least-once delivery is the honest guarantee for an external effect without provider-side idempotency. For invitations a repeated email contains the same still-valid link, so duplicates are harmless; later producers must state their own tolerance.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Send after commit in the request
text:
Send after commit in the request
Simplest, but a crash or relay outage after commit silently loses the message, and retrying inside the request ties panel latency to the relay. Rejected by the delivery policy for required effects.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: PostgreSQL job library
text:
PostgreSQL job library
Libraries such as pg-boss provide queues on PostgreSQL, but they own their schema and its migrations. Fitting that schema into the repository's reviewed SQL migrations, semantic metadata and least-privilege runtime grants would need adaptation and ongoing tracking of the library's internal tables. A small owned table covers the current need with explicit semantics. This was assessed from the libraries' documented design, not by a trial integration.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Broker or Redis-backed queue
text:
Broker or Redis-backed queue
Adds stateful infrastructure, backups and monitoring on the single host for low volume, and still needs an outbox to close the commit gap.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Provider HTTP API with webhooks
text:
Provider HTTP API with webhooks
Offers delivery events and bounce data, but couples code to one provider before PH-17 selects it and may require paid procurement. Can be reconsidered when a provider is chosen and bounce handling is needed.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
An email intent commits or rolls back with the change it reports, and survives restarts and relay outages.
No new infrastructure beyond the existing API and PostgreSQL; the provider stays replaceable through configuration.
Delivery state is queryable, so the panel can show failures and offer resend.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
Duplicate emails are possible after a crash; every producer must tolerate them.
Dispatch stops while the API is down, and the API process gains a background loop to drain, monitor and test.
Without bounce processing, "sent" means accepted by the relay, not delivered to the mailbox.
The outbox holds personal data and short-lived encrypted secrets, which need retention, cleanup and key rotation.

title: ADR-0026: Deliver Transactional Email through a PostgreSQL Outbox and an SMTP Relay
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
New `RESTRICTED` settings (relay credentials and the outbound-mail key ring) and monitoring of queue age and failures. Real sending requires PH-17's sender, domain authentication and provider terms, and PH-13's notices; local and CI use a disposable Mailpit sink.
Moving dispatch to a separate worker later reuses the same table and claiming rules; adopting a provider API later replaces only the adapter.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
text:
ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
**Status:** accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-19
**Acceptance scope:** The owner explicitly approved this decision and the nine decisions of the device enrollment and lifecycle design on 2026-10-19 under PH-22. Acceptance establishes the direction for local and CI implementation of PJ-08 with simulated players, not Android player delivery (PJ-12), hardware qualification (PH-08) or production readiness.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Context
text:
Context
Teluni screens are Android TV players without a keyboard that must be paired to one company and branch by a person who is already signed in to the panel (FR-02). Policies require temporary, single-use, rate-limited codes that are safe under concurrent claims, a separate revocable identity per device that is never a human principal, revocation that denies future server access, and no custom cryptography or token schemes ([security requirements](../project/security-and-i18n.md#pairing-and-device-lifecycle), [release policies](../project/release-policies.md#offline-authorization-and-clock-trust)). Keycloak holds only human identities ([ADR-0024](0024-propose-keycloak-and-server-managed-human-sessions.md)), and the pilot runs on a single host ([ADR-0021](0021-propose-a-single-host-pilot-with-portable-persistent-storage.md)).
This record decides how a device is enrolled and how it authenticates afterward. The detailed rules, limits, data and contracts are in the [device enrollment and lifecycle design](../project/device-enrollment-design.md).

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Decision
text:
Decision
Teluni will enroll devices with an application-owned flow shaped like the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628) and authenticate them with a device-generated bearer credential:
The player generates a 256-bit credential from the platform CSPRNG, keeps it in Android Keystore-backed storage and sends only its SHA-256 when it starts an enrollment. The API answers with a short user code to display and an enrollment ID to poll.
A signed-in, authorized person enters the user code in the panel; one conditional transaction claims the enrollment and creates the device in the chosen company and branch.
The device then presents the credential as a bearer token on device routes only. The API stores only the hash, resolves it on every request without caching, and revokes it by state change. Human routes never accept it and device routes never accept a human session.
User codes are short-lived, single-use, stored only as a keyed HMAC and protected by attempt limits.
The API's devices module owns the flow; the shared runtime gains only a `device` operation access kind. No identity provider, certificate authority or proof-of-possession library is introduced now.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Rationale
text:
Rationale
RFC 8628 is the established pattern for input-constrained devices, so the user-facing shape and its code guidance (alphabet, length, expiry, rate limits) come from a reviewed standard rather than invention. Generating the credential on the device means no secret is ever returned by the server, so a lost response at any step is retried without issuing anything and without a re-issue path. A 256-bit random value needs only a plain hash for storage and lookup. A bearer credential over HTTPS fits the single-host pilot and the existing Fastify/PostgreSQL stack.
The accepted cost is that a copied credential is usable until revoked, unlike a key that never leaves hardware. Revocation on the next request, rotation and the `device` access kind as a single seam keep a later move to proof of possession contained.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Alternatives Considered
text: Alternatives Considered

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Server-issued credential returned at pairing
text:
Server-issued credential returned at pairing
Returning the only copy of a secret in one response makes a lost response either a stuck device or a reason to add a re-issue path with more secret-bearing responses.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Device key pair with signed requests or mutual TLS
text:
Device key pair with signed requests or mutual TLS
DPoP (RFC 9449) or client certificates would keep the private key in hardware and resist copying. They add proof verification or certificate issuance and renewal without a measured threat that requires them in the pilot. They remain the preferred upgrade if PH-08 devices offer usable hardware-backed keys and the threat model calls for it.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Keycloak device grant and service accounts
text:
Keycloak device grant and service accounts
It reuses an established server, but makes each screen a Keycloak client or user, couples player operation to Keycloak availability and mixes device and human identities that the policies keep apart.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Consequences
text: Consequences

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Positive
text:
Positive
No secret leaves the server, and every enrollment step is safely retryable.
Revocation is immediate for reachable devices and needs no token lists or expiry windows.
Device and human authentication stay separate at the operation level.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Negative
text:
Negative
A credential copied from a compromised or rooted device works until revoked; physical control of a player remains a residual risk, as the security requirements already state.
Teluni owns the enrollment endpoints, limits and their tests instead of relying on an identity provider.
A new `RESTRICTED` key ring for user-code HMACs must be configured and rotated.

title: ADR-0027: Adopt Device-Generated Credentials and Code-Based Enrollment
heading: Operational or Migration Impact
text:
Operational or Migration Impact
Host migration and restore must preserve credential hashes so devices keep working, without ever exporting the credentials themselves.
Moving to proof of possession later requires a player update and an overlap period in which both schemes are accepted for already-paired devices.

title: ADR Instructions
heading: ADR Instructions
text:
ADR Instructions
Consult the [decision index](README.md) and [authoring policy](authoring.md) before creating or changing an ADR.
Start new proposals with the [template](template.md) and `proposed` status. Acceptance is distinct from implementation completion.
Preserve accepted rationale, decisions, dates, and stable identifiers. Architectural changes require a new decision and explicit supersession, not rewritten history.
Retain meaningful alternatives, negative consequences, constraints, and evidence. Do not invent evaluations to fill the template.
Update current policy and reciprocal supersession references when an accepted architectural change requires them.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
text:
Authoring Architecture Decision Records
Use the [decision index](README.md) to search existing decisions and the [template](template.md) to draft a record. ADRs preserve decision history and rationale; current policy describes current architecture. Git, migrations, changelogs, design documents, and runbooks retain their separate responsibilities.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: When a decision needs an ADR
text:
When a decision needs an ADR
Create an ADR for a significant choice whose rationale a future contributor cannot reliably infer from implementation. Relevant effects include system boundaries, dependency direction, ownership, runtime/deployment topology, security, persistence, public contracts, cross-cutting technology, operational behavior, and long-term maintainability.
Consider the breadth, reversibility, long-term dependency, plausible alternatives, integrity/security implications, and risk of losing the reasoning. Ordinary local refactors, fixes, tests, small helpers, individual indexes, and routine dependency additions do not each need an ADR. Major technology choices generally do. Existing foundation policies do not each need retroactive ADRs.
An ADR records a sufficiently concrete architectural conclusion, not every discussion or rejected idea. It must not become a task tracker, changelog, runbook, detailed implementation design, or snapshot of volatile vendor data. A separate RFC system is not required. Bundle decisions only when their rationale and lifecycle belong together; avoid giant records deciding unrelated parts of the stack.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Lifecycle and historical integrity
text:
Lifecycle and historical integrity
Status
Meaning
`proposed`
Under active consideration; implementation must not assume finality unless explicitly exploratory
`accepted`
Approved architectural direction; implementation and current documentation should align, allowing an explicit migration period
`rejected`
Considered and deliberately not adopted
`superseded`
Previously accepted, then replaced by another decision; link the replacement
`deprecated`
Historically relevant but no longer appropriate for new architecture; use sparingly when replacement is transitional or incomplete
Do not add statuses without a clear need. Normal transitions are proposed to accepted/rejected and accepted to superseded/deprecated. Do not normally revert historical decisions to proposed; create a new record when reconsidering them.
Accepted does not mean implemented or released. Track pending/partial/completed implementation through normal issues, tasks, or pull requests, not extra ADR statuses. Exploratory work and proofs of concept provide evidence but do not themselves establish acceptance. Long-lived production implementation should generally not rely on an unresolved major proposal.
Accepted substantive history should remain immutable. Non-semantic spelling, formatting, broken-link, and obvious-typo corrections may be acceptable, but must not change historical meaning. When architecture changes, create a new ADR. Retain the old record, mark it superseded, and add reciprocal `Supersedes` / `Superseded by` references. Keep the original date. For partial supersession, identify precisely what remains valid, what changed, and which decision replaces it.
Rejected records can preserve useful evaluation and constraints; a changed context can justify reconsideration in a new ADR. Do not treat rejection as a permanent prohibition. Purely local abandoned proposals may be removed before meaningful shared history; preserve broadly reviewed or referenced proposals as rejected where useful. Do not record every immediately dismissed idea.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Identity and metadata
text:
Identity and metadata
Use monotonic numeric identifiers and descriptive English filenames of the form `NNNN-short-decision-title.md`. Numbers identify records, not importance, domain, priority, or version. Gaps are acceptable. Never reuse or renumber identifiers already in shared history. Resolve parallel numbering conflicts before merge; an unshared identifier may be changed.
Record title, status, date, context, decision, and consequences. For accepted records, the date should generally be the acceptance date. Titles should describe the decision rather than merely name a topic. Preserve identifiers once merged and referenced.
Simple Markdown metadata is the current format. `pnpm docs:check` validates filenames, matching titles/IDs, status, ISO dates, required sections, and index membership. Preserve these field names as tooling contracts. Supersession semantics still require review; no automatic numbering or supersession checker is implemented. ADR files remain canonical; avoid duplicate status stores or custom ADR software without a concrete need.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Content and evidence
text:
Content and evidence
**Context:** explain the actual problem, relevant constraints, scope, timing, and assumptions. Avoid unnecessary implementation detail.
**Decision:** state the chosen direction clearly enough to understand independently of the alternatives.
**Rationale:** explain the material tradeoffs, evidence, and constraints. Distinguish confirmed evidence, reasoned tradeoffs, and assumptions.
**Alternatives:** describe serious alternatives considered; do not fabricate alternatives or evaluation evidence to fill a template.
**Consequences:** include benefits, costs, limitations, new responsibilities, security/operational effects, and reversibility or migration costs where relevant. Formal scoring is not required.
**References:** link relevant repository policy, earlier decisions, designs, benchmarks, proofs of concept, and durable evidence. Avoid unnecessary dependency graphs and large volatile datasets. Preserve enough explanation that disappearing external links do not destroy the rationale.
Use current evidence at decision time when product capability, support lifecycle, pricing, security status, or provider limits matter. Vendor documentation can support constraints but must not be the sole location of the explanation. Detailed implementation and operational migration steps normally belong outside the ADR.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Creation, review, and acceptance
text:
Creation, review, and acceptance
Search the index and related policies for the same question, accepted direction, superseded decision, or rejected alternative. Determine whether this is an architectural decision rather than an implementation detail.
Allocate the next available identifier, copy the template, and use `proposed` status.
Document context, explicit direction, meaningful alternatives, rationale, constraints, and positive and negative consequences while the context is still known.
Review in proportion to impact: is the problem real, the complexity justified, and the choice consistent with existing architecture? Identify conflicts and intentional deviations explicitly.
Accept or reject through repository review. For a small team, review, merge, and accepted status are sufficient; do not add governance ceremony without a concrete need.
On acceptance, update affected current documentation and implement the selected direction with relevant verification. Do not retain rejected experimental paths unnecessarily.
For supersession, additionally identify changed constraints, reciprocal references, affected current policy, and compatibility/migration work. For rejection, record decisive reasons, preferred alternatives where applicable, and conditions that could justify reconsideration.
Retrospective ADRs should say the decision was already in effect. Record only known reasoning and state uncertainty rather than inventing a historical evaluation. Significant principle deviations belong in the decision and corresponding current-policy update. When later accepted decisions supersede older records, follow the replacement and current policy rather than treating the superseded record as current architecture.

title: Authoring Architecture Decision Records
heading: Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
text:
Maintenance and deferred mechanisms
Routine maintenance should be limited to permitted corrections and supersession metadata. Current architecture must remain discoverable without reading the entire chronological ADR history. Keep descriptive titles, explicit technologies/concepts, and useful related references.
Frontmatter, automatic numbering, generated indexing, status/supersession validation, approval workflows, and required reviewers remain tooling or organizational decisions. Introduce them only when justified. ADRs should preserve meaningful reasoning without becoming bureaucratic records for every change.

title: Architecture Decision Records
heading: Architecture Decision Records
text:
Architecture Decision Records
Use this index to locate governing decisions without reading the full history. Each linked record owns its status, decision, rationale, and consequences. Acceptance does not imply implementation; see [validation availability](../validation.md) and the [technology map](../architecture/technology-decisions.md).
For a new decision, read [authoring policy](authoring.md), inspect related records, and use the [proposed template](template.md). Current behavior belongs in the [policy index](../README.md), not in rewritten historical ADRs.

title: API Error Contract
heading: API Error Contract
text:
API Error Contract
[Task index](../README.md) · [API principles](principles.md) · [Error handling](../architecture/error-handling.md) · [Compatibility](versioning.md)
This policy owns public failure semantics. The API's [shared error registry, envelope schema, and responder](../../apps/api/src/errors.ts) and each composed module's registered codes are canonical; the [public registry composition](../../apps/api/src/error-registry.ts) gives each code exactly one owner and rejects any duplicate, even an identical definition, and the [generated error reference](../generated/api/errors.md) lists implemented codes, messages, categories, HTTP statuses, and retry classifications. Module route contracts declare expected operation errors. Follow [ADR-0007](../adr/0007-establish-api-contract-openapi-sdk-and-configuration-schema-strategy.md) when generating OpenAPI and SDK representations.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Envelope

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Format
text:
Error Code Format
Public codes use stable semantic `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` names. Clients branch on codes and deliberately defined structured fields, never on message text or internal exception classes. Messages are safe human explanations and may change for clarity or product localization without changing the code's meaning. Canonical repository descriptions remain English.
Infrastructure identifiers such as SQLSTATE, ORM codes, provider exceptions, filesystem paths, or runtime class names are not public semantics. Map failures to the condition consumers need to understand. Reuse an existing code for the same meaning; do not create a code for every code path, collapse materially different consumer actions into one generic code, or reuse a retired code for a new meaning.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Error Code Ownership
text:
Error Code Ownership
The feature/application owner defines business failures; the API boundary owns cross-cutting public mappings. The registry provides one canonical definition, and operation metadata refers to it. The registry enumerates stable public conditions, not every possible database/network/library exception. Do not maintain an independent manual registry in prose or generated clients.
For a new code, determine its semantic owner, expected/unexpected category, public disclosure safety, consumer action, status mapping, retry implications, optional details, and compatibility impact. Update canonical code, operation declarations, tests, and generated references together. Each module's implementation conventions explain its authorization-sensitive classification order.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Validation Errors
text:
Validation Errors
The implemented validation response is `400 VALIDATION_FAILED` with the common envelope. Do not expose validator exceptions or echo submitted values. Structural validation is distinct from a valid request that conflicts with current domain state.
If field-level details become useful, add an explicit bounded schema to the canonical contract. Identify fields using a stable public request-path convention, never internal database/ORM paths; use stable reason codes where clients need to act and safe human text for explanation. Define multiple-failure bounds and unknown-field behavior. Returning every issue in an attacker-controlled payload must not create an unbounded response.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Mapping and disclosure
text:
Mapping and disclosure
HTTP status conveys broad protocol meaning; public codes convey application semantics. The [generated registry](../generated/api/errors.md) is the current status mapping. Validation uses `400`, authentication `401`, permission denial `403`, absent/hidden resources `404`, state/version conflicts `409`, rate limiting `429`, unexpected failures `500`, and service unavailability `503` where declared.
Authentication and authorization failures follow their [security policies](../security/authentication.md). Avoid account enumeration and disclosure of hidden resource existence, cross-tenant data, claims, or policy internals. An absent and inaccessible resource may deliberately share `404`; test that behavior.
Expected domain conflicts, stale versions, and incompatible idempotency-key reuse are explicit outcomes. Distinguish safe replay from a conflicting new intent. They should not become internal incidents simply because code represents them as exceptions.
Translate known database constraints at the persistence/application boundary according to business meaning. Unexpected database failures stay unexpected; do not disguise every exception as invalid user input.
Translate provider business rejection separately from dependency unavailability, configuration failure, or unknown outcome. Expose vendor-specific distinctions only when consumers need them, never raw provider content.
Use a safe generic error for unexpected failures. Never serialize arbitrary exceptions, stack traces, SQL, secret values, internal paths/hostnames, or diagnostic dumps. Do not return ordinary API failures as hidden error objects inside `200` responses.
Public status is not internal severity: expected denials may matter to security monitoring, and a transient dependency failure may be operationally serious. [Error reporting](../reliability/error-reporting.md) owns that distinction.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Unknown Outcome
text:
Unknown Outcome
A timeout, disconnect, or commit error may leave the caller uncertain whether a write or external effect occurred. Retryability cannot be inferred from HTTP status or transient infrastructure failure alone. Define whether the operation is known not to have occurred, safely replayable, or requires state reconciliation. Introduce a distinct public unknown-outcome code only when consumers need different handling.
A public retry hint, if introduced, must be machine-readable, bounded, and accurate for the operation. Rate-limit guidance must not disclose anti-abuse internals. Never imply a non-idempotent write is safe to repeat merely because the registry classifies a failure as transient. Each module's recovery conventions own its create replay and mutation reconciliation behavior.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Details and additional delivery modes
text:
Details and additional delivery modes
Every public details object needs a typed schema and a consumer purpose. Include only information safe for that caller; omit record dumps, protected resource/tenant identifiers, authorization evaluation, credentials, and provider payloads. Cross-cutting correlation/retry metadata should remain distinguishable from domain details. Once consumed, field meaning and shape are compatibility-sensitive.
When additional modes are introduced:
Mode
Error requirement
Webhook or upload
Follow the operation/provider contract while minimizing signature-validation or scanning details. Bound and classify upload failures explicitly.
Asynchronous work
A successful acceptance response does not guarantee eventual success. Externally visible job status maps worker failures to stable public semantics, never worker exceptions.
Batch/partial success
Define atomic versus partial processing and item identity in an operation-specific result. Do not ambiguously overload the ordinary single-error envelope.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Diagnostics and consumer behavior
text:
Diagnostics and consumer behavior
Report an unexpected occurrence once at its authoritative boundary. Preserve useful internal causal evidence only within [redaction rules](../security/telemetry-redaction.md); preservation never authorizes raw exception-message or stack export. The current runtime records allowlisted diagnostic fields rather than arbitrary error content. Expected validation, business, and access failures may contribute to safe metrics/security/audit signals without becoming unexpected incidents.
Clients and SDKs must preserve structured error semantics and correlation, and provide a safe fallback for unknown codes. Application consumers should not depend on framework-specific transport exceptions for business meaning. Product code decides whether to display safe server copy or localized client text; it must not parse that copy. The current thin SDK exposes generated response/error typing without adding a separate error-class hierarchy.
Code meaning, status mappings, details, categories where consumed, and retry behavior require [compatibility review](versioning.md). Adding a code can break exhaustive consumers; renaming/removing a code or changing meaning is potentially breaking. Optional details are only additive if actual clients tolerate them.

title: API Error Contract
heading: Change and verification checklist
text:
Change and verification checklist
Inspect the registry, similar conditions, owning operation, actual consumers, authorization/disclosure policy, and compatibility commitments.
Define the safe semantic mapping and outcome/retry behavior. Add details only when needed, with explicit schema and size limits.
Verify the real transport envelope, status, code, safe message, correlation, hidden-resource handling, and relevant failure paths. Test absent/invalid/expired credentials and other lifecycle states only where that mechanism exists.
Inject unexpected failures and assert that secrets, SQL, provider data, input values, stacks, and internal paths do not escape. Verify one appropriate diagnostic event and safe retry metadata if present.
Regenerate and check the registry/OpenAPI/SDK references through [validation](../validation.md). Preserve current checks for registered unique codes, operation declarations, and freshness; extend checks for any new detail schemas or released compatibility obligations.
